title: Five Ways to Increase the Effectiveness of Instructional Video https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11423-020-09749-6 https://tipsforteachers.co.uk/research-five-ways-to-increase-the-effectiveness-of-instructional-video/
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 19, 2024 — original paper:
summary: This page covers Mayer, Fiorella, and Stull's review of their own programme of research on what makes instructional video effective, distilled into principles supported by empirical evidence. The dynamic drawing principle favours drawing graphics live on the board over presenting pre-drawn ones, particularly for low-knowledge learners, and the presence of a visible drawing hand appears to matter. The gaze guidance principle recommends looking at the camera or audience while talking and shifting gaze to the board to signal where students should look next. The generative activity principle encourages building in note-taking, explanation-writing during breaks, or imitation of the instructor's actions, which especially help low-knowledge learners. The seductive details principle -- consistent with Barton's other research pages on this topic -- warns against interesting but extraneous video content that distracts from deeper processing. Finally, for second-language learners, subtitles paced slowly enough to avoid overloading working memory are recommended. Barton notes the authors frame these as evidence-based but still tentative guidelines, open to further refinement.
points: Drawing graphics live on the board (dynamic drawing), rather than presenting pre-drawn graphics, helps learners -- especially low-knowledge ones -- focus on what matters, and a visible hand appears to help.
Teachers should use gaze guidance -- looking at the audience, then shifting gaze to the board -- to signal where students should look.
Generative activities during video lectures, such as note-taking, explanation-writing in breaks, or imitating the instructor, particularly help low-knowledge learners.
Avoid seductive details -- interesting but extraneous video content -- since they distract from deeper cognitive processing.
Subtitles help second-language learners, provided the video's pace is slow enough not to overload working memory.
quotes: This brief review of our research on learning with instructional video shows that progress is being made in developing evidence-based principles for how to design effective instructional video

Dynamic Drawing Principle: Rather than presenting pre-drawn graphics, teachers should draw graphics on the board as they lecture. This is especially important for low-knowledge learners, as it helps them focus on the important information in the lesson
Gaze Guidance Principle: Teachers should look at the audience while talking and shift their gaze to the board to signal where students should look
These could include taking summary notes during a video lecture, writing explanations during breaks in the video lecture, imitating the actions of the instructor during a video demonstration

Seductive Details Principle: Teachers should avoid adding interesting but extraneous videos to their lessons. These can distract learners and prevent them from engaging in deeper cognitive processing during learning
When students are viewing an instructional video in their second language, teachers should add subtitles and make sure the pace is slow enough not to overload working memory
